## "Association Between Chronic Exposure to Sodium Nitrite and Colorectal Neoplasia Development: A Prospective Cohort Analysis"

---

**Background:** Sodium nitrite (E250), widely used as a preservative and color fixant in processed meats, has been hypothesized to contribute to carcinogenesis through the endogenous formation of N-nitroso compounds (NOCs). While the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen in 2015, the independent contribution of sodium nitrite remains insufficiently characterized.

**Objective:** To investigate the prospective association between estimated dietary sodium nitrite intake and incident colorectal cancer (CRC) risk over a 12-year follow-up period.

**Methods:** This prospective cohort study drew from 104,568 participants (aged 35–70, free of cancer at baseline) enrolled in a national dietary surveillance program (2010–2022). Dietary sodium nitrite exposure was estimated using repeated 24-hour dietary recalls (minimum 6 per participant), cross-referenced with a proprietary food composition database quantifying additive concentrations across 3,500+ commercial products. Participants were stratified into quartiles of cumulative sodium nitrite intake (Q1: <0.05 mg/kg bw/day; Q4: >0.15 mg/kg bw/day). Incident CRC cases were identified through linkage with national cancer registries and histologically confirmed. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, physical activity, alcohol consumption, smoking status, total caloric intake, fiber intake, family history of CRC, and overall processed meat consumption (to isolate additive effects from other meat-related exposures). Sensitivity analyses employed substitution models and restricted cubic splines to assess dose-response relationships.

**Results:** During 1,047,233 person-years of follow-up, 1,143 incident CRC cases were documented. Participants in the highest quartile of sodium nitrite intake (Q4) demonstrated a statistically significant elevated risk of CRC compared with the lowest quartile (Q1) (HR = 1.24; 95% CI: 1.06–1.46; p-trend = 0.003) after full adjustment. The association was more pronounced for distal colon and rectal cancers (HR = 1.31; 95% CI: 1.08–1.59). Restricted cubic spline analysis suggested a non-linear dose-response, with risk elevation becoming apparent above approximately 0.10 mg/kg bw/day. Stratified analyses indicated stronger associations among participants with low dietary vitamin C intake (HR = 1.38; 95% CI: 1.11–1.72), consistent with the known inhibitory effect of ascorbic acid on nitrosation. The association was attenuated but remained borderline significant (HR = 1.16; 95% CI: 0.99–1.36) when further adjusting for total processed meat volume, suggesting partial independence of the additive effect from other meat-matrix components.

**Conclusions:** Higher dietary sodium nitrite intake was associated with modest but statistically significant increases in CRC risk, particularly in individuals with low antioxidant intake. While residual confounding cannot be fully excluded in observational designs, these findings support further investigation into sodium nitrite as an independent contributing factor in colorectal carcinogenesis and may inform regulatory re-evaluation of permitted usage levels.

**Keywords:** sodium nitrite, food additives, colorectal cancer, N-nitroso compounds, prospective cohort, processed meat
